Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: George, a 67-year-old widowed interior designer of Oceania ethnicity, was captivated by his traumatic experience of captivity. The memories that suddenly surfaced often felt like an ambush. For instance, he would be working on a new design project when the memory of being held captive in an enclosed space would intrude, accompanied by the chilling sound of shouting in Arabic—voices he had never heard before but which now echoed through his mind. These intrusive memories and auditory triggers profoundly influenced George’s behavior. He began to avoid enclosed spaces entirely, choosing only open rooms where he could ensure that no one could approach him from behind. This avoidance extended to his work environment; he would often skip meetings or avoid crowded design presentations. At times, he would rehearse what he was going to say in advance of any interaction, as if preparing for a confrontation. The feeling of vulnerability and the vividness of these triggers heightened George’s sense of threat. He became convinced that danger could arise at any moment, especially in enclosed spaces where he felt trapped and unable to defend himself. This constant vigilance led him to feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall, from which he could survey his surroundings. The sensation of vulnerability also intensified his negative emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame—which made it difficult for him to navigate daily life. George’s memory of the captivity was complex. He could recall what happened in detail but often felt emotionally numb, as if the events had occurred to someone else. When he tried to recount these experiences to others, he found himself struggling to articulate his thoughts coherently. The auditory memories—the shouting and other sounds—were particularly distressing and often left him feeling overwhelmed. These intrusive memories and their emotional numbing contributed to George’s heightened sense of threat. He felt that his body reacted to danger before he could even process what was happening, leaving him in a constant state of hypervigilance. This fear reinforced the cycle, making it more difficult for George to revisit or fully engage with the traumatic memories. Over time, these maladaptive strategies and heightened threats began to affect George’s daily life significantly. His avoidance of enclosed spaces and rehearsals before interactions made work increasingly challenging. Colleagues noticed his absence from important meetings and presentations, leading to a decline in his professional reputation and increasing feelings of isolation. What finally brought George to seek help was the realization that these behaviors were starting to take over his life. He was most afraid that he would continue to avoid necessary social interactions and work commitments indefinitely, isolating himself further. Yet, he also harbored hope for relief from the constant vigilance and intrusive memories. His deepest fear was losing his sense of self entirely, but he clung to the possibility that with help, he could regain control over his life. George’s journey through this trauma had led him to a crossroads where seeking professional assistance seemed like the only way forward. The intricate web of triggers, maladaptive strategies, threats, and memory disturbances had created an overwhelming burden that he now recognized as unsustainable.
